chunks: From him, from Ali al-Jarimi, from Durusta al-Wasiti, from Ibn Muskān, from al-Hasan ibn Harun, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I said to him, 'I ate khabeeṣ (a type of bread/dough) containing saffron until I was full.' He said, 'When you have completed your rituals and intend to leave Mecca, buy dates with one dirham and then give them in charity; it will be an expiation for what you ate and for what entered upon you during your state of iḥrām that you are unaware of.'

key_terms.إِحْرَام: Iḥrām, the sacred state of consecration entered by pilgrims.
key_terms.خَبِيص: Khabeeṣ, a type of bread or dough made from flour and water, often cooked.
key_terms.دِرْهَم: Dirham, a silver coin used as a unit of currency.
key_terms.زَعْفَرَان: Saffron, a spice used for flavoring and coloring food.
key_terms.كَفَّارَة: Kaffārah, expiation or atonement for a religious violation.
key_terms.مَنَاسِكَ: Manāsik, the rituals and rites of Hajj.

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for eating saffron-flavored food while in the state of Ihram during Hajj?
ai.summary: In this narration from al-Isṭibṣār, Imam al-Ṣādiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that consuming saffron-flavored khabeeṣ violates the prohibition of using scented items during iḥrām, requiring a specific expiation of charity. This ruling highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on compensating for both known infractions and any unknown violations (mā lā taʿlam) that may have occurred during the pilgrimage rites. The use of a dirham for dates reflects the practical application of fidyah in the context of minor iḥrām breaches.
